# Front Upper Control Arm Replacement — 2023 Model 3 RWD

**Vehicle:** 2023 Tesla Model 3 RWD
**Job:** Front upper control arm (FUCA) replacement, driver side
**Reason:** Knocking noise from the front left over broken pavement, worse at low speed

> All torque values, part numbers, and clearances in this document are
> `[PLACEHOLDER — verify against the service manual]`. This file exists to give
> the chunker realistic prose structure, nothing more.

## Symptom and diagnosis

The noise presented as a single sharp knock from the front left when crossing
expansion joints at low speed, and disappeared entirely above roughly 40 mph.
It did not change under braking, which pointed away from the brake hardware.
Steering feel was unaffected and the car tracked straight, so a tie rod was
unlikely.

With the front end supported and the wheel off, grabbing the upper control arm
and working it vertically produced audible play at the ball joint. The lower
arm and the sway bar end link were both tight by comparison. On this platform
the upper control arm ball joint is not serviceable separately, so the arm is
replaced as an assembly.

A useful cross-check before ordering parts: bounce-test each corner and listen
for a repeat of the knock. A worn upper arm on a Model 3 typically knocks on
rebound rather than compression.

## Parts and tools

- Front upper control arm assembly, driver side — part number `[PLACEHOLDER]`
- Replacement hardware: knuckle pinch bolt and two arm-to-body bolts. These are
  torque-to-yield on many suspension components and should not be reused.
- Torque wrench covering `[PLACEHOLDER]` N·m
- Ball joint separator, or a soft-faced dead blow
- Metric sockets, `[PLACEHOLDER]` mm for the arm bolts and `[PLACEHOLDER]` mm
  for the pinch bolt
- Jack stands rated well above corner weight

## Procedure

Raise the front of the vehicle at the designated lift points and support it on
stands. The Model 3 has reinforced pads in the sill; using anything else risks
crushing the rocker. Remove the front wheel.

Locate the upper control arm where it meets the top of the steering knuckle.
Remove the pinch bolt securing the ball joint stud, then separate the stud from
the knuckle. If it resists, a few sharp taps on the knuckle boss beside the
stud will usually release the taper without damaging the boot on the new part.

At the inboard end, the arm attaches to the body with two bolts. Support the
arm before removing the second one so it doesn't drop. Note the orientation of
any alignment cams before disassembly — reinstalling them rotated changes the
camber setting.

Install the new arm inboard first, hand-tight, then seat the ball joint stud
into the knuckle and start the pinch bolt. Torque everything only after the
suspension is loaded at ride height. Torquing bushings at full droop preloads
them in the wrong position and shortens their life considerably — this is the
step most commonly skipped and the reason some replacements develop noise again
within a year.

Final torque: arm-to-body bolts `[PLACEHOLDER]` N·m, pinch bolt `[PLACEHOLDER]`
N·m.

## What to check afterward

An alignment is required after replacing any control arm. Camber and caster
both shift, and driving on it uncorrected will scrub the inner shoulder off a
front tire in a few thousand miles.

Road-test over the same surface that produced the original noise. If a knock
remains, suspects are the sway bar end link, the lower control arm bushing, and
the strut mount bearing — all of which produce a similar sound and none of which
are ruled out by replacing the upper arm.

## Notes for next time

Buying the arm and the hardware together avoids a second delay when the
torque-to-yield bolts turn out not to be in the box. Doing both sides at once
costs one extra arm and saves a second alignment.
